title: Google Scholar as a data source for research assessment
venue: Springer Handbook of Science and Technology Indicators
extended_summary:
The provided paper is not the requested secondary-school writing study. Instead, it is a handbook chapter examining Google Scholar as a source of bibliographic and citation data for research assessment and bibliometric analysis. The chapter asks how Google Scholar works, how large and diverse its coverage is, how it differs from traditional databases such as Web of Science and Scopus, and what limitations it presents for scientific evaluation.

The chapter does not study an educational intervention, writing instruction, or AI-assisted feedback. Its approach is descriptive and analytic: it explains Google Scholar’s indexing model, inclusion criteria, source types, citation-linking process, and secondary products such as Google Scholar Citations and Google Scholar Metrics. It also synthesizes empirical evidence and presents large-scale analyses of Google Scholar’s size, source coverage, geographic and document-type diversity, and citation relationships with other databases.

No participant population is studied in the sense required for an education intervention paper. The chapter discusses researchers, students, librarians, publishers, repositories, and institutions only as users or sources within the scholarly communication ecosystem, not as subjects in an intervention study. The context is global scholarly communication and bibliometrics rather than a school, classroom, or writing setting.

The main conclusion is that Google Scholar offers a broader and more inclusive view of the academic world than selective databases because it indexes a much wider range of document types, languages, and sources. At the same time, the chapter argues that this breadth comes with substantial limitations for evaluation purposes, including instability, lack of transparency, metadata inconsistencies, and difficulties in reproducing results. The authors position Google Scholar as a supplementary—and in some fields potentially preferable—source for research assessment, but not as a perfectly controlled bibliometric database.
quality_tier_rationale: The provided text is a handbook chapter about Google Scholar as a bibliometric data source, not an empirical K-12 writing intervention study. It does not evaluate any educational technology intervention on secondary students, report a study sample, or provide outcome data on writing skills.
impact_tier_rationale: No student learning intervention or writing outcome impact is studied in the provided text, so there is no evidence of positive educational impact to rate.
